generated_note: Curated by hand from public advisories. Every entry below cites the NVD record plus at least one primary source (research paper or vendor advisory). See SOURCE.md for the format and SCHEMA.md for field semantics. Detection rules are deliberately conservative: when fingerprint data is not a definitive indicator, confidence drops to 'low' and severity is held at 'info' or 'medium'.

entries.name: KNOB, Key Negotiation Of Bluetooth

match.rationale: Pre-5.1 BR/EDR implementations did not enforce a minimum encryption key length; the spec allowed negotiation down to 1 byte. Bluetooth SIG erratum 11838 (Core 5.1) introduced a 7-byte minimum. Confidence is medium because some vendors backported the fix without bumping the LMP version.

entries.description: BR/EDR encryption key length is negotiable down to 1 byte, allowing offline brute force of the link key after capturing a single session.

entries.name: BIAS, Bluetooth Impersonation AttackS

match.rationale: BIAS exploits the BR/EDR Secure Authentication procedure: a device that supports Secure Connections on the controller but does not enforce mutual SC authentication against a peer claiming legacy is impersonated. Bluetooth Core 5.1 (errata 11838 + 12009) tightened this. Confidence is low because feature-bit presence does not tell us whether the host enforces SC; live probing is the only reliable check.

entries.description: BR/EDR authentication can be downgraded to legacy, letting an attacker impersonate a previously-paired device without knowing the link key.

entries.name: BLUFFS, Bluetooth Forward and Future Secrecy

match.rationale: BLUFFS abuses session key derivation in BR/EDR Secure Connections: the attacker forces a weak diversifier so past and future sessions share keys. Bluetooth SIG erratum 23976 (Core 5.4) closes it by binding the diversifier. Confidence is medium because LMP version 5.4 is still rare in deployed devices and the fix requires both controller and host updates.

entries.description: Session key diversification in BR/EDR Secure Connections can be forced low, breaking forward and future secrecy across pairings.

entries.name: BLURtooth, Cross-Transport Key Derivation downgrade

match.rationale: When the peer advertises CT2 (CTKD willing) and accepts Legacy Pairing, an attacker can negotiate a weak Legacy LE LTK that the stack then derives into a BR/EDR link key, downgrading the cross-transport security. Bluetooth SIG erratum 11838 + Core 5.1 mitigations added; not every host enforces. Confidence medium because deriving usable BR/EDR access also depends on host-side BR/EDR support being enabled.

entries.description: Cross-Transport Key Derivation can promote a weak LE pairing key to a BR/EDR link key, breaking the security guarantees of either transport.

entries.name: BIAS variant, BR/EDR Pin-Pairing impersonation

match.rationale: BR/EDR PIN-code Pairing on Core 5.1 and earlier allowed an attacker to complete authentication without knowing the PIN by exploiting the reflection of IO capabilities. Core 5.2 + erratum 16980 tightened the procedure. Confidence is low because only legacy pin-pairing devices (rare on modern peripherals) are affected, and the LMP version alone cannot confirm pin-pairing is in use.

entries.description: Legacy BR/EDR PIN-Pairing on pre-5.2 controllers is susceptible to an impersonation flow that completes pairing without the PIN.

entries.name: Invalid Curve attack on LE / BR-EDR Secure Connections

match.rationale: Affected implementations failed to validate the peer's ECDH public key during LE Secure Connections (and SSP), letting an active MITM recover the link key. Affects iOS pre-11.4, macOS pre-10.13.5, BlueZ pre-fix, several SoCs (Broadcom, QCA, Intel). Confidence is low because the fingerprint cannot prove the stack lacks the public-key validation patch; it only narrows to peers offering SC without MITM, the surface the attack uses.

entries.description: Implementations of Bluetooth Secure Connections that fail to validate the peer's ECDH public key allow an active MITM to recover the LTK.

entries.name: BlueDuck / forced unauthenticated BLE-HID keystroke injection

match.rationale: Multiple BLE HID host stacks (Android, Linux, macOS, iOS) accepted pairing from a forced peripheral that claimed HID + no-input-no-output IO capability, then immediately accepted keystroke reports. Patched by Google in December 2023 and by Apple in iOS 17.2 / macOS 14.2. Confidence is low because the fingerprint cannot confirm the peer exposes the HID GATT service (0x1812); operators should cross-check with recon/ble_target_enum and look for the HID service.

entries.description: BLE HID stacks could be coerced into pairing with a forged peripheral, after which keystroke reports were accepted without further authentication.
